extracted.intended_audience: authors and reviewers on Royal Road and other online fiction communities
extracted.subtask_description: A short community guide explaining how to write and interpret reviews for online serial fiction, covering the main review segments: style, story, grammar/vocabulary, and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is defined not by the qualities of the story, but by how the story is presented. Though some people may disagree, Style is not subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good style should be consistent in its perspective and should not change; a strong sense of chronology is a must. Examples: a first person story should stay in first person even when switching to someone else's point of view; scenes should be presented in their intended reading order (A→B→C) or deliberately reordered (B,C,A) with clarity. Weak chronology or inconsistent perspective can create 'time gaps' and confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent Perspective / Point of View
rubrics_metrics.description: A story's narrative perspective should remain consistent and not switch arbitrarily between first and third person or between different narrators without clear reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: switching from first person to third person (or vice versa) without justification; endless rapid switching between perspectives (unstable perspective). Good practice: maintain a coherent POV or clearly signal and justify changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology / Timeline Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong chronology ties scenes together into a flowing, pleasant read; weak chronology creates confusing 'time gaps' where events happen but readers can't place them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present scenes in a clear order; if changing chronology, do so deliberately and clearly. Unstable chronology (presenting scenes in an order that obscures intended sequence) is damaging to presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story — overall (plot, characters, setting)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good story has a fun plot, interesting and entertaining characters, and a well-defined setting in which it takes place. A setting need not be complex to be well-defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story requires some kind of plot (not merely 'girls' busts' or superficial fanservice). Evaluate whether the plot is engaging and whether characters and setting support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should have believable motivations for their actions; sources of motivation must make sense relative to the stakes and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: very few people would realistically 'risk their life in another world against a Demon Lord' without a credible motive. For serious stories, motivations should be serious and convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Plot Devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot devices should be coherent, foreshadowed, and meaningful (e.g., a need to gather magic artifacts before the villain obtains them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good plot devices drive story tension and make sense within the setting. Assess whether devices create logical stakes and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak Plot Devices / Deus Ex Machina (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak plot devices like deus ex machina, unexplained power-ups, and un-foreshadowed twists undermine story credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unexpected power-ups that lack explanation, plot twists with no prior setup, or the main character winning when they shouldn't. These diminish tension and reader investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Plotless Fanservice ('girls' busts')
rubrics_metrics.description: A story that lacks any plot beyond sexualized or superficial elements is weak even in harem/ecchi comedy contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in genre stories, there should be narrative purpose beyond repeated fanservice; otherwise the story will feel empty and unsatisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonist Motivation / Justified Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who oppose the MC should have real, understandable reasons to do so rather than being 'all evil jerks' with no cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly motivated antagonists feel cheap and reduce story stakes. Ensure antagonists have plausible incentives or conflicts with the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slice-of-Life Scenes for Character Development
rubrics_metrics.description: Slice-of-life scenes (small everyday details) are important for building characters by showing likes, dislikes, and personality through routine actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of such scenes can damage character development; include small moments that continuously build the character over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting Logic Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal logic of the setting must be consistent and not contradicted by later events (e.g., a water magic stone shouldn't later be burned if rules forbid it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: contradicting established rules for convenience (e.g., later chapters violate earlier stated limitations). Maintain coherent rules or explain exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and Vocabulary — importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar is something writers must work on; vocabulary is vital and often overlooked. A larger vocabulary keeps prose fresh and less repetitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits of larger vocabulary: more enjoyable reading, better descriptive scenes, reduced repetition, and improved reader perception of author skill. Smaller vocabulary can make writing feel repetitive and drain freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Grammar Mistakes (reference list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent errors to watch for include misuse of it's/its, your/you're, they're/their/there, possessive nouns ('s vs s'), affect/effect, do's/don'ts, i.e./e.g., peek/peak/pique, alot/a lot/allot, and comma vs period misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list to check basic grammar and word-choice errors; they are common and can harm reader perception even if the plot is good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters — relationships with depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should have deep relationships (rivalries, love interests, friends) that add dimension and interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether relationships feel developed and contribute to character arcs rather than being superficial labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must act consistently; abrupt flips in feelings or behaviour within a short span are harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: a character hates something one moment, loves it the next, or shows fear in one scene and no fear the next without explanation. Maintain believable psychology and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Stereotypes vs 'Stereotypical Stereotype' (proper use of archetypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes (archetypes) can be used, but authors should avoid overused, shallow portrayals—termed 'Stereotypical Stereotype'—which are cringe-worthy when abused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good use: well-defined, non-stereotypical takes on archetypes (e.g., true definition of tsundere or yandere rather than clichéd caricatures). Bad use: flat-chested tsundere who just yells 'baka' and hits the MC whenever shy. Stereotypes can be effective if used thoughtfully; overuse makes them hard to use well.
